title: What is terror management theory?
summary: Josh and Chuck open by discussing a Conservation Letters paper by Conservation International's Will Turner arguing that climate mitigation and unpreparedness can harm tropical forests and species, such as hydroelectric dams causing ecological and seismic problems. They then explore how media coverage of climate change leans on alarmist language, citing a UK Institute for Public Policy Research review of news articles, and how fear messages can backfire (a Northwestern binge-drinking PSA study and a 2009 cigarette pack warning study by terror management theorists). The core of the episode explains terror management theory, rooted in Ernest Becker's Denial of Death and developed at the University of Missouri in the 1980s, covering distal and proximal defenses, the judges study on prostitution sentencing after mortality reminders, and why alarmism may cause people to disengage. The episode closes with a listener mail segment from teachers at Mountain Ridge Middle School in Colorado Springs whose eighth graders produced their own podcasts, and a sign-off.

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck introduce the episode with light banter about their chemistry and the topic of the week.

segments.title: Conservation paper on climate change and tropical forests
segments.summary: Josh describes a Conservation Letters paper by Conservation International's Will Turner arguing that human populations displaced by sea level rise could plunder tropical forests and endangered-species sites. Chuck and Josh then discuss how dams built as clean energy can cause earthquakes, lake formation, and downstream damage.

segments.title: Public belief in climate science and media disconnect
segments.summary: The hosts note that a PNAS study of climate scientists found broad agreement that human-caused climate change is real, and discuss a Gallup poll finding Americans increasingly think global warming is exaggerated. They attribute part of this to media alarmism and professional skeptics.

segments.title: Alarmist language in UK climate coverage
segments.summary: The hosts describe a UK Institute for Public Policy Research review of news articles that found alarmist language was the most common framing of climate change, with quotes from James Lovelock. The review also identified pragmatic and non-pragmatic optimism as other categories. The hosts note correlation was shown but not causation.

segments.title: Fear messaging that backfires
segments.summary: The hosts discuss a 2010 Northwestern study in which guilt and shame PSAs about binge drinking increased drinking among some viewers, and a 2009 Journal of Experimental Social Psychology study in which aggressive cigarette pack warnings increased smoking in some people. The 2009 study was conducted by terror management theorists.

segments.title: What is terror management theory
segments.summary: Terror management theory was developed in the 1980s by psychologists at the University of Missouri, building on Ernest Becker's Denial of Death. Becker argued culture distracts people from death, and that encountering other cultures can prompt hostility. The theory distinguishes distal defenses, such as clinging to one's culture, from proximal defenses, such as downplaying threats. A judges study showed that mortality reminders led judges to harsher prostitution sentences.

segments.title: Applying terror management to climate doom messaging
segments.summary: The hosts discuss how terror management might explain disengagement from doomsday climate messaging, and suggest the media adopt a pragmatic optimism approach. They mention the CFL mercury coverage as an example of alarmist reporting that discouraged small actions.

segments.title: Listener mail: eighth graders' podcasts
segments.summary: Teachers at Mountain Ridge Middle School in Colorado Springs write that their eighth grade class produced its own Stuff You Should Know-style podcasts. The hosts play a short clip of a student episode about dim sum.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts invite listener theories by email, point to the website for more information, and close the episode.
